This means numbers originally were "little endian" in human language, and still are in right to left languages. So even "natural" isn't accurate. 🙂 That being said, I think there is value in most-significant-first because it makes skimming easier. excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: I sparked unintentionally a debate over endianness but didn't get an answer to my naive question: is there a reason to have `Bytes32` for `base_fee_per_gas` instead of `uintN`? In the latter case, for all purposes within the CL it would be encoded as 32 bytes little endian (as long as N<512) but clients would have to deal with the contents as an arithmetic type.

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<dannyryan> Uints in ssz are encoded as little endian
CL doesnt have to do any computation on this value so idea is to just encode it as bytes so that no translation has to occur betwern layers
Otherwise it would have to be translated as it crosses EL/CL boundary

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: But if you have it as uint it will still be encoded anyway as 32 bytes little endian, and no translation has to ocurr between layers. And eventually, if the CL actually merges completely and we have to deal with this field, it is better to have it now as an uint than have to change it later.

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
CL clients don't support int types larger than unit64. No computation is done on the type in CL. Thus to avoid the requirement of a larger type, it uses a forward compatible bytes typing

Succinct statement by proto to this fact here
https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/2550#pullrequestreview-730802682

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: I think it'd be fine to make it uint256 encoding especially if we avoid computation on it as it's just an encoding format rather than a big-int computational requirement

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<protolambda> - SSZ supports uint256
- CL avoids uint256 for now, for simplicity
- We picked bytes32 in CL, to not deal with uint256 typing
- We picked little endian here, so we can change from bytes32 to uint256, without changing anything but the type (encoding is the same)
- The API is tricky though, because the JSON RPC has a distinction between data and quantities. In the JSON-RPC we respect the EL practices, so there it is encoded as a 256 bit quantity, which is big-endian.
- See earlier discussion and specs issue about overflowing this field if it were a uint64. It would be super expensive, but it's still theoretically within reach, especially if it's performed with ETH on some chain that nobody is going to build on, but which is rather just created to create chaos.

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: right -- your second to last point (as I note above) makes it seems less worthwhile to have this bytes32 mis-direct on the CL type

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: because the CL client must at least be able to parse the integer value in some fashion for sending to EL

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: thus CL is aware of 256-bit integer encodings (but not 256-bit integer arithmetic 😅 )

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <protolambda> Also note that quantities in the API have no leading zeroes. So whatever endianness the bytes32 value is, there's some conversion regardless

excerpts.author: paulhauner
excerpts.content:
The Bytes32 does indeed feel pretty weird in LH.

We have a Uint256 type that we use to parse the value from the EL, and then cast that into a Bytes32 (with endianness swap).

We already have SSZ impls for Uint256 since it’s so easy to reason about in SSZ.

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content: <protolambda> Defining it as a uint256, but just not using arithmetic on it, so client implementations can be simple for now when necessary, might be best

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: but if using uint256 is not problematic at all, it's cleaner to have it now than to change it later
